blocks.x: All right, now, we're talking to Earl Humphrey. Today is November 30th, 1968. Now, could you tell us about when you were playing with Buddy Petit? What is all you can remember about Buddy Petit?

Well, I suppose it must have been just about 1926. And we had a gig over in Mandeville every other Saturday night. In the hotel. Buddy was stationed over there with another man. And it looks as though he had gotten tired of being over there, kind of lonesome, just working on weekends. So he decided to come home and join us in the Orleans with Lee Collins and Earl Humphrey's band. That was our band. So you mean you had two companies? We only had one until Buddy joined us. So Buddy, he got on the train. We wasn't expecting to come over with us. Anyhow, when we looked around, the train had gone. Buddy had slipped on the train. Anyhow, come on over. Now, naturally, we had a little work. And he stayed with us for about two months. And then he decided to go back to Mandeville. But during the time he was with us, we did pretty well.
Tell me, what's George Lewis in that band?
George Lewis was in that band. George Lewis was in that band.
George, can you tell, who else was in the band? Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. and little dad, Vincent, Turner Banja, Roy Evans on drums, Earl Hunter, myself on trombone, Lee Collins on trumpet, and with the addition of Buddy, maybe we had two trumpets for us. Yes.

And a seven-piece arch. Well, now in this story, it's slightly different from the story I've had before, because I've heard that you played with Buddy, or he played with you in George Orson's song. Then you had some kind of a, you know, Buddy didn't get on with Buddy or something, and you fired Buddy, and you got Lee Collins after Buddy left. No, I don't remember that.

You don't remember that? Oh. But I do remember playing with Buddy when he had his band just extra, when his trombone player was sick. That was quite a while ago, before he went to Manaville. He had a popular officer out there until he went down. Yeah. But before he was fine, Buddy, that didn't happen. Those buddies made up his mind he wanted to go back over to Manaville where his wife was. So, he was working over there,
and that's what he did. So, really, you only played with him for quite a short while. Before then, no, I had. You had not played with him.

Not for quite a while, because the only time before then I'd play with him, as I told you, see, when his trombone player was sick, while then I'd play a gig, you know, and stuff like that did he. Yeah. And his band. Yes.
So, what was his band? Was that the, um, written, the Black and Tam band?
No, that was the original,
Buddy Petit's band. Yeah. He had the most popular
jazz band around at that time
when he had his band. Right. Who was in that band? Do you remember?
Yeah. Morris French on trombone.
And, uh,
well, he had two, three different drummers, but the face of it was one of his drummers.
And he had, uh,

Buddy Manning on the band. Zeb, Ezeb Lenoris and Kleines. And, uh, Simon Maruero on bass violin. He had a six-piece band. Well, in case of him, he'd use the piano, well, he'd use what we call it, Tink. Xavier Batiste's piano. Yeah.
What did you think of Alfred Freddie as a trumpet player?
Good.
He was one of them. What, what, what, do you describe him about his style or anything like that?

Well, it's hard to describe. He'd probably, mostly have to hear the fellow's play. That's right. I'm afraid we won't be able to do that album. He played on a difference between, well, between Lewis Armstrong and, of course, the old-time great. and,
uh, the old-time great. He had, he had,
he had a style of his own, he just went to see. Yeah. Yeah.
Did he sound anything like Buck?
Well, something like Buck. Buck Johnson. Yeah, some, some phrases. Yeah. Yeah, some like Lewis Armstrong. Yeah. And then he had a good many ideas of his own. Yes. Frazes.

There was some, you know, there's some story I read in some book somewhere that there's a chance that he may have made some home accordings in Thibodeau. Did you ever hear anything about that? No, I didn't. I haven't heard anything about any of his recordings. I mean, nobody's ever found them, you know? No, well, I, I, I don't know. It's just a rumor that they may exist. I was just wondering if you may have heard something about that. Did he ever play out there? Thibodeau? Yeah.

Well, I suppose still, but he's bad to go from one, you know, town to another, the wheels, 20 to 200 miles, you know? Yeah. Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, different places like that. Yes. Weekends, it's like you're doing that, you know?
Well, when you were playing with Buddy and George and so on, over, when you came over here for a short time, whereabouts did you play?
Oh, we had one regular Sunday night job, B. St. Paul. That's, just before you get, it was, just before you get into Jefferson Parish. Yeah. Just on the other side of the 17th Street Canal.
Well, what was that job?
Trayvon,
yeah. What was the job? Can you describe it?
Yeah, it was a baseball park, but they had a pavilion.
Yeah.

Played baseball practically every Sunday up there, and then after the ball game, why, then they'd have a dance, they had a pavilion, you know, platform with top on the dancing. I see. And we played for all the occasions they had up there, whether it was football or baseball, anything they had, we were there.
Was that your job?
Yeah, that was the house band. You know,
like I have a regular house band,
we was a park band. Yes.
Were you the leader
of the band? Manager.
The manager.
The manager.

What was the band called? Well, Humpy's band. Oh, it was called Humpy's band. Yeah. And what sort of numbers would you play? Almost ragtime, a few poplars, mix them up. Did you have any special numbers or any numbers that... No,
we didn't have
any special outstanding numbers. We tried to make them
all that way. But she was young, eh? There's more family could do more than, you know, like I could, like up there now, I could feel

that stuff. Yeah. Yeah. Tell me, how did George Lewis sound in those days? Good. Wonderful. Oh, he did. Really? Yeah. Would you say he sounded much the same as he does now, or, I mean, was his style? I mean, you know, he was younger and all, I understand that. Yeah,
well, he naturally improved his tone a lot.
Yeah.
And, yeah, well, he has improved. Yeah. He has improved. But he was good then.
And always a hard worker. Yes. He must have been quite young then, too. I mean, he was...
Well, 1926 or 27, I don't got which now, but it's right long in those times.
I thought, oh, I hate to, because you were there and I wasn't, but I think that this must have been a little bit before that. Before 26?
Yeah,
I would say.
It might have been.
It's been so long I can't, but it's been long there. About 24, maybe. Something like that.
Time passed so fast, you know, until you can't exact get the, you know, the years on things, like that.
Now, what date, I remember I was reading this interview with you in the, you know, this doctor or somebody did an interview with you out in Charlottesville?
Yeah.
Um, you mentioned the date you left New Orleans. Do you remember that?
Yeah.
What was that?
March the 31st in 1931.

31? Yes. Now, this is what I want to ask you, because this is, it's unusual for someone to be able to remember a date very precisely like that. So, when you left New Orleans, was Buddy Petit alive or was he dead? Buddy Petit was alive. He was alive. Yeah. Now, do you know when, did he die soon after you left or did you hear when he died or did you hear anything about it? No, he didn't die
soon after I left. I don't know exactly when he died, but he was around a good while after I left.
He was. Yeah. Did you, did someone send you a postcard or anything? Did you hear it when he died?
Oh, he didn't hear anything about it until I come back in 1941.

Really? Didn't he? You didn't hear anything about it? No. Because, you see, he is supposed to have died on July 4th, 1931, which would be two or three months after you left. Now, I don't know whether that date's right, but the reason why they say that is because that's supposed to be the year Louis Armstrong came down. Yeah. He said he was a pallbearer. Right. That's what they said.
Well, you see, I wasn't here. I couldn't give you no direct date on that.

But anyway, he was, that's one thing anyway, because he definitely didn't die. I was thinking, Dorf Lewis was saying to him the other day he thought he may be about before 1931, but he obviously didn't, that he was still alive. No, he was still alive. Yeah. Okay, well, that's something anyway. I have one thing I wanted to ask you about. You're reading some of this, and this is something this man interviewed before asked you about before. When they had some of these old, these dancers, you know, and they'd have the real lowdown music, slow music, and he said, there'd be this thing about some kind of music that'd start a fight.
Oh, yeah.
Now, what I can't understand, and Bill Russell asked me about this, what we can't understand is, what is it, was it something about the music that would start the fight?

I know, but see, it's the time that we played, you know what I mean? We'd have a break, you know, half hour break, you see. While I'd do it all that time, well, the cats would be drinking, you know. during prohibition time, but they always wasn't bootlegged. Yeah. And they'd get half stewed up, you know, it didn't take much to start a fight after then, you know, it'd be probably after 12 o'clock, or the other after one, when we supposed to play until two, sometime later. Yeah. Well, we'd play this particular piece, Dirty Air Myth, and that was a kind of slow piece, and kind of battle-out stuff, see, and they'd get the rubbing together, and one grabbed the wrong one, the gal, or something like that. Well, that's where, that's mostly where it started. It's where it started, while the police would break it up, because it's so, you know, soon you're breaking up time many, I'll probably have another hour. Yeah. You would end starting.
You would deliberately play this number? Oh, yeah. Yeah,
we knew what's coming up.
What was coming up? Yeah.
Sometimes we'd miss it, but very subtle. Yeah.
Now, what was that number you said? what's that Dirty MF? Now, is that a blues? Is that a blues?
Yeah, it's a blues, low-down blues.
Does it have any particular melody or any particular? No, Can you hum it at all?
That song is, yeah.
That's pretty good. I never had that one before. I don't know whether they played that one.
Yeah, some of the bands played.
It sounds a bit like that blues that I believe Chris Kelly used to play.
That's Chris Kelly's band I was playing with then.

It used to be as funny as the good ones. Yeah. And with that thing that you were humming there, was that the trumpet part? Yeah, that's the starry blues. And I know that it was this blues that they recorded, and of course Chris Kelly never made any records either, but this record that they made in 1943 with Kit Howard. Supposed to have played a little bit like him.
Yeah, well he played that.
Yeah. And he plays this careless love, and then before the careless love, they have this blues. Yeah. With the da-da-da-da-da-da, da-da-da-da-da-da-da. Well that's the same thing. Sounds like...
But he put the careless love, the only one in there. Right.
Yeah. Well, tell me something about Chris Kelly, because he's another one who's never recorded and so on. Oh, he's a swell trumpet bell, man. That line of...

He had a style of his own. Yes. Hard-working man. Wonderful tone. He was just a all around good jazz trumpet bell. Awesome. He didn't overdo nothing. Awesome. He used various kinds of mutes. Yeah. Whereabouts would you play with him? Oh, we played all over Louisiana. Different places, lots of fraternities and dances. Mm-hmm. All the halls down there. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.

Yeah. such as the Corporatees Hall, the Economy Hall, the New Hall, the outdoor lawn forties. That used to be a pretty great company. Besides, we did lots of work out in the Irish Channel, some up in the university, country clubs.

Who was playing with Chris Kelly when you were playing? Who was on time there? Zeb Miller. Zeb Lanois? Yeah, Zeb. What about, aren't you Milly Bones supposed to have played with Chris Kelly? Maybe he played with him a little bit.

Well, now that was a different band. When Milly Bones, I played with Milly Bones, that was Johnny Brown's band. And Johnny Brown was a kind of involuntary. Milly was the better kind of up there, so he used to use Milly Bones and himself in his own band. That was Johnny Brown's band. And their regular trombone player was Mr. Harris. But most times on the weekend, he was a baller maker. And they called him overtime. Well, he didn't steal his job, you know. And he'd always get me to go in his place. Johnny Brown's band.
Harris.
Yeah, Harrison. Harrison.
Oh, I see. It's Harrison Barnes. No, not that. This is Harrison.

I forget his name. That's his last name, Harrison. He lived in Algiers. Oh, it's his last name? Ray Trombone player. I never knew his first name. That's all I used to call him. Harrison. Yeah. I see. Who were, at that time, in the twenties there, who would consider the outstanding caranac guys
in the U.A.s, would you say? Well, always, take Piku, Loretta Teo, Charlie McCready, and the other guy, and the other guy,
you know, down that line like that.
How was George Lewis rated amongst the kind of friends at that time?

He was related. He's always, everybody always recognized him from, from when he first started to playing, I'll tell you, like, all kind of good old musicians always recognized his playing, you know, see? He would never know Hamlet, like he'd come out playing. Yes. Did he, when he come up? When he first started, he was playing good. Yeah. Of course. When he got acquainted with the musicians, that he played. Yeah. Why did you leave the city? Well, it's about two things. One thing, I wanted to get away from around my wife. I leave town, that was one thing. And, when I was working, it was hard work at the Levita dance hall, with Jenny dancers. And then, I could make a little more money on the road. No expenses, see I did. Oh. The larger paid bus, two meals a day. And, about half more money than I was making on here at this workhouse, Levita dance hall.
Well, that's what made me.
And, I had been a traveling man, you know, on different shows anyhow, so, in the spring of the year, coming around, I always feel like moving. Oh. Which I did for a long time.
When you left here, did you, were you, were you meaning to stay away that long? No.

No, I had been going and coming back, about every year, probably every two years. But, this time, out of the way, the depression kind of slipped up, you know. The boys down here wasn't doing anything. And, where I was, that, the first time I went in Jamaica, Georgia, in the winter, 1931, 32. Pickens was pretty good around there. That was a make a living, see.
You were playing fun by that?

Yeah. All I could hear out here, things, closing down, and pressuring, and start to creep up on people, water, no need me coming back here. I could make it, around Macon, Georgia, different places that stopped in the winter times. Oh.
Things that tighten up, you look pretty good. Yes. Were they getting bad before you left? Yeah, it was tight. Yes.
You could tell. I stayed on the road, they, they held up, of course, they cut the sours down.
Who were you traveling with, exactly?
Well, that, that, that particularly, I was, I stayed with them three years. Florida Blossom Minstrel Show, one-nighter.
Oh.
Your Minstrel Show.
Well, what, what was the, who would have been playing, I mean, what was the, you were playing from band, what other musicians were you?

Oh, we had about twelve piece band, brass band, because they played for the shows too, you know. Yeah. We had twelve pieces, twelve, at the time fourteen. Really? The show consisted of about thirty-five, forty people altogether. Man, women, chorus girls, singers, comedians, violets, and...
But was it like a circus?

Yeah, like a circus, under a tent. Tent, big, spread a big tent. Yeah. Every day, move every day. The sun, the way I was gonna show on Monday, while then they move in there that Sunday morning, see. We'd be there Monday morning. That's the only time to stay two days. Very seldom with your, uh, theater, well, when we did a three, theater day, why, we'd stay there three days.
Yeah. It just... Gosh, it must have got towering, all that moving, all that moving, all that moving, the tent around, and all that...

Well, they... ...packing, you know what? They had regular men to do that. All we did was play. And instead of the storm come up, well then everybody's pitching, you know, trying to up the loaded tent to keep from destroying it. Well, then we didn't do anything. And we were sleeping vans right on the same lot where the tent would be for us. Yeah. Well, right out, you're sleeping thing right in the tent. And we had a canvas tent cookhouse.
We had breakfast and supper. So... Um, when did you actually give up playing? I mean, or more or less, we know...

Oh, when I stopped, uh, I stopped in just about to see... I shipped about... ...45. Something like that. When we were... When we were... When I stopped playing trombone, then, I went to playing piece and... ...played a little piece of violin, a small combo over there. Where was that? So Sam took over the rest of the boys to make the combination sound that would be head while I shipped to piece of violin. Oh, I see. I lived in Charlottesville, Virginia. Hmm. Went to the... Who were you playing with, uh, or did you say, uh... Well, we had a common... A small combination, such as piano, two saxophone, and drums. This was in Charlottesville. Yeah.
Oh, really?
I didn't remember to say... And, uh... I used to live near there. I was just teaching school there. Yeah. A place called Woodbury Forest. Yeah, yeah. Yeah. It's near Orange. Sure.
We used to play in... Civilities. No, it's not military school. There are lots of military schools. But there are lots of military schools. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. Lots of military schools around there. Yeah. But this one wasn't a military school. It was a private school. Yeah. It was a real nice place. Yeah. I played that. Up on the middle hill. Yeah. Did you play that? For... For... For... For a school. For a dance. Yeah. Oh, I wish I could have... I could have had you. Yeah. We...
We all run a good... VMI... VPI... We had lots of playing in Richmond. Richmond. Jesus Boy.
Now were you playing, these talks you're telling me about, were you playing song right then? Yeah, we had a good, you know, a big band.

We had about ten pieces and a full piece. And you were playing song? Yeah, that's before the second world war came out. Yeah. You know, split the band up. Man of age, you know, for the war. Yeah. Cut it down. Yeah. Just about five pieces. Well, we didn't have any other brass, so I switched to face fire.
Any particular reason for coming back to New Orleans? Yeah. What was that?

Well, the first thing I lost my wife in 1958. And she died. And I stayed around there and straightened out the building, that's one thing or another. And my father was here sick. He was invalid, about 14 or 15 years. My aunt was likewise. And I had a slight heart attack. Well, I couldn't work on the job I was working on. They let me go on the job. On economy sickness. And they also went to, well, they just, they decided that I go on the, uh, on the social care. See, they just built the social care. And, uh, if I had that on my mind, and I could come down here and help my sister with my father and do, I'd be better off here. Yeah. Yeah. And I was around there just, they weren't practically anything at all, see. So, I just come on back. What now? I didn't have any children, no relatives, anything.
Oh.

And Bill and Percy, they had a, they had a thing in Washington, a musical or a jazz festival, something like that. And me being 117 miles from Washington, my brother Willie sent me a telegram and said they'd be over there. And I went over there to see them, and after they explained the situation to me, I thought it would be anything else for me to do. But get things straight on that end and move on back in. Oh.
Well, now you've been away for 30 years. About 30 years. Yeah. How much change have there been in New Orleans in that 30 years?
Oh, lots of change, plenty.
Yeah.
But I used to come back, see, about, the longest time I stayed with was the first 10 years. I was 31 to 41. But after then, I'd come back about every two years.
Oh, really? Yeah. What are the main changes that have taken place in that?
Oh, well, the growth of the city, that's a big thing. And then, the main thing, of course, most of that happened since I've been there, is integration. That's one of the great things.
Oh, right.
Is it noticeably different? Yeah, it is. It's a thing.
Oh, right. You mean, is it different in the places you can go to or in the attitude of people? Well, it's both.

The attitude of people. Some, you know, what I would say, just about most of the people's attitude. A little different. Yeah. Yeah. Of course, they always will die hard, you know. Yeah. Yeah. They ain't going on with different places and different stuff. Yeah. But I think it's much better. Yeah. And that's one of the big differences. The sirens are so much better. Yeah. People are living, they're living better. They're glad they're living in better homes and comfort. So that's, that's what I would call the greatest change. Yeah. Most of that happens since I've been there. Yeah.
You think it has in the last six years? Yeah. You've noticed a change in the last six years? Oh, yeah. The last three years. Yes. Sure. What about the music?

Well, the music, yeah, the music has changed most of it. But that's all over. Different, different styles of music, you know. Of course, it's Dixieland music like we play. That hasn't changed any. But such as the modern jazz and the rock and roll system and the other systems. Well, that's changed a lot. The people are going more for that than they, they would, you know, years ago. But they're really going for that kind of music. Now, you're younger generation, they're going for it. So that's a big change in that style of music. Now, you call it, your first music you've heard is Dixieland. You call it, is that what you call it, Dixieland? Yes.

Dixieland or Ragtime. When did you call it, I mean, when, did you call it Dixieland back in the thirties, twenties? No. It's a jazz band. It's just a jazz band. Yeah. It's just a jazz band. Yeah. Dixieland or Ragtime. Yeah. Dixieland or Ragtime. Dixieland or Dixieland. Dixieland or Dixieland.
Oh, ragtime. Ragtime, my jazz. Of course they had different types of bands around there. Then for a while they had 10, 12 piece bands. Well, they played, you know, mostly off the street.

You playing tomorrow? We'll just let this tape run off. We're going to take a little break and then do the other side. I just want to, I want to watch that channel. So I'll have to get a bit of time. Okay.
Hey, I just did it. You know what I'm saying? I need to do it. I'm here. I hope I'm going to make it to my yard. I'm here. I'm here.

I'm here. I'm here. I'm here. Okay. Well, now what should we talk about? Yeah, this is one thing which I'm interested in. It's very difficult to tell from just listening to records. Is whether the music, overall, the music, you think the music has changed over the years? The style. I mean, I'm talking just about the style. What you did. Dixon's. Well, not the Dixon language.

We had to change. It had to change. Not to my family. Yeah. Not the real old players have changed the style. No. But the young people have changed some of the styles of playing, such as the blues, Marlick Jazz, Rocky Roo.

Oh, yeah. Some other kind of a... But now, the thing is, if you listen to some of those old records, now this is what... I just have to go by the records, you see. But if you listen to those bands, now they only recorded a few of the bands down here, like, well, Louis Domaine, who was playing with, and Sam Morgan's band. Celestan. Celestan, yes. Celestan. Of course, the Perron Orchestra. Well, let's just take the Morgan band. To me, the Morgan band sounds to me like the style is nearly the same, but it's not quite the same. It seems to me like there's a little bit of change there.

Well, you know what I believe, and you don't make the difference. See, it's more modern equipment now for recording than it was then. Yeah. You get a... You can get better reception on what you're playing, you know, off of this modern equipment, than you could then. Yeah. That makes a big difference, see. They can phrase your music like they want on one of those, you know, regular recording of phrases. Well, before they didn't have all that.
Yeah.

You couldn't even design the drum beat on a... And bass violin was... that wouldn't take. If it did, it was so faint, it wouldn't help, you know, it helped the band playing, see. But you couldn't hear it on the records. Oh. Not so playing. Yeah. Kind of put a blur in the music, but what you did hear, see. Oh. That's when most of them went to using sousaphone, recording bass and track.
Yes.

And see, that, that, that, I imagine, which I know, made a big difference. And hearing the band off the record while, during that time, the only thing you could hear was the cymbals and the wood blocks. Uh-huh. And every now and then you could hear the snare, but the bass drum just wouldn't, wouldn't go on. Uh-huh. I don't know whether you ever noticed that.
Yes, that's true.
Well, that made a difference.
Tell me about the recording you made, as I was to make. Do you remember that?
Yeah, I remember making a record, but I can't remember the name of the pieces.
I really, I don't, I've only heard those records once or twice, eh?

I have, uh, I have, uh, the fact I had one, I went to somebody around here, because I haven't got a clear. I've forgotten now who I learned it to. Yeah. A fellow and, uh, the doctor, you know, and Virginia gave me the record, you know, a small, a small album. Yeah. And, uh, did you rehearse for that session? No. I hadn't paid in about a month when the nurse came to me.
I just put, put the horn up doing construction work. And they come by and asked me.

And, you know, just run over my horn again. But I came, well, the work was scarce then, and I wasn't, with no organized bands. So I went on doing construction work. And they come by and asked me. And, you know, just run over my horn again. But I came, well, the work was scarce then, and I wasn't, with no organized bands. So I went on doing construction work.
Now that was in 1926 when you made it. That was 26. Remember you said the other day it was 26 with Buddy?
Yeah, 26 or 27. I, you know, I can't, can't think of the dates. Yeah.
So now, when you were playing with Buddy then, that was before when you made it. Yeah.
Yeah, before then. Because I went off on the road that night. Yeah. I'd gone down to Crowley, Louisiana, playing with the Black Eagle, playing.

Yeah. Another thing it seems to me, there were certain bands, maybe this is true, there were certain bands that maybe had a style more on like today's style. I mean, they just weren't ever recorded. You see, like, take Chris Kelly or Buddy the T, you know, they were recorded. Yeah, they never recorded. And it seems like they were probably had more, more swing, more jazz to them. You know, you'd say some of those bands, like Sam Morgan's band, or more, or, of course, the Piron band, you know, it was just more straight. That's a different kind of orchestra, yeah, sure.

Well, it's like I tell you, see, all, all the bands, now you listen to them around there every night. It's a different than every band come in there. But it's similar on the same style, but no two musicians in town plays exactly alike. Not only in town, that is when you routine it. No two or no place plays exactly alike. But they're similar, you know, you can tell, you can distinct, tell that you, it's similar to the others, you know. But it's not exactly alike. You get used to them, you can stand outside and tell, tell, just who's in there, who's playing in there. See, you can be around them long enough. Of course, it's similar on the same style, all right, but it's different in there. It's hard to explain what's different, but there is. Yes.
Well, let's talk a little bit about your very early days of the band. What were the very, very first jobs you played?

Well, the first jobs I played, I played with a fellow named Dan. He was a guitar player. And he used to have a four-piece band, go out on the lake on Sundays. That was most of his work. Every Sunday he'd have a departure train that was lit up at little, uh, uh, places out there that was dancing. You know, what they called, uh, regular dancing places, you know, camps. You know, camps, you know, out in the water, about, some of them out there about, probably a block of air. Go out on the run, man, and porch all around the cabin, see, people dance all around. Well, that's the first job that I remember playing with him. That is, other than playing around with my grandfather, you know, giving concerts, churches, and different things like that. We did lots of that before. We went out. Where was that? Right here. We was living in that house right back there. Yeah. We'd give concerts and churches, hall, and different things like that.
What sort of music would that play?
Oh, we'd play just some light serenades, overtures, a few marches, hymns.
It would be more like classical music.
Yeah, more semi-classical and hymns. Yeah. We'd be back there at a family band. Were you reading? Yeah. Were you reading music? Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah, I really did. Did you ever hear any of those real old time players like, um, Samuel Perez? Yeah, I worked with man.

I worked with man at Temple Roof Court for about six or seven months. Yeah, he was a man up there. What's one of the style of he called? Oh, he was mostly a business trumpet player. But he had his own style of jazz. He was very loud, wonderful tone, you know. Professional trumpet player. Oh, boy. He's the best I've ever been around here.
Did he play jazz? Some people say he played more straight, played more straight.
He played more straight, but he jazzed in his own style, you know. Oh. Yeah.
What about King Oliver? Do you remember?

Yeah, but I was small when King Oliver left the hour and he played. But to tell you anything about his playing other than listening at his records, nah, I couldn't tell you. Because I was real small when he was that guy. Yeah. Couldn't get around much, you know, being so young, you know.
When were you born? 1902, September 9th. What about, um, did you ever hear any music in the district? Yeah. Did you ever play that?

Yeah, I paid Pete Lottie's wife. Cabaret. Paid for the played on Iville Street. The beans in about five or six months. Where was that at? Well, in Iville, between, uh, Ramport, not Ramport. Yeah. Ramport, every time. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. No, beans' place is on this side. It's in Ramport. Between Ramport and, uh, Ramport, something like that. Dauphine, I remember.
Who did you play with? Who were you playing with?

And there I was, I was waiting with Charlie Love, Joe Robichill, drummer for Marl. I'm Shreveport, I forget his name. I don't know what I call him. Always call him Nose, that's all I remember his name. Can't think his name. And, Kim will wake with us a while, he was just starting up. Well, uh, now he came with him. Yeah. I think he was going to school at the time. I wish I was.
Who were, now what about trombone plays? What styles did you, did there any, were there any particular people you, uh, you thought were particularly good or anything?
Yeah, well I always, my, my presence was always kid or anything.
Did you, you, you heard him playing him right in your own?
Oh yeah, I heard him play, I used to, I heard him play, he was, nice, great, I did.
Was he considered one of the best trombone plays? He was, the best trombone.

And his style of playing, of course they had better, and the musician, line, he was lots better, lots of them are better than him, but in his style of playing, and, you know, and his Dixie Ray, and J.S., Ragtime, whatever you make, or he was the best. That is to me, I, of course, there was always some good ones around me. What were the things about his style that you took really long? Well, he was a smooth player. Wonderful ideas about faking music. Wonderful. What do you mean by faking music? Well, a person not being able to read any.
Yeah.
The experience, direct, from the, you know, listening and making his own chords. Good chords, but he used them to his own instincts, you see.
Well, do you ever hear your music as a question of singing, Thornburn? Yeah. Yeah.

That's, uh, you may call it a straight drum, or play leads, or vibration. Yeah. Lift drills, and lift things like that. That's my idea about singing. Yeah. And playing, I guess. Mostly the lead, and, yeah, kind of melody. Yes, that's right. Not too much fapping, you know, like we used to do.
Yeah. What is, uh, what do you, what do you, what do you, what do you take that's fresh from the tailgate?

Oh, well, that come from when we used to advertise. In fact, every Sunday, there'd be four or five bands out on the street, advertising for the dance, either that Sunday night, or probably that next night, which would be a Monday. Yeah. Right, then, the fierce fouls would sit on the left-hand side, the back of the truck. You know, after you let that tailgate down, well, that's where the drum bone and the fierce fouls would be out there. That was their piece on that truck, a particular truck. All right? That's where that expression come from. Yeah. Teargate, I imagine. That's all I can figure.
To me, now, the word is used, it's also used in a, to denote a real style.

Yeah, well, most of the guys that played that, uh, see, it's in a vamping style, see? And most of the bands that did this advertising, most of all the trombone players, playing on it, you know, vamping style. No singing trombones. Just regular vamping.
Would you demonstrate that, like, humming or something? What do you mean by vamping style?

Well, just, well, I can just tell you, it's mostly a bass, a bass part, you know? You play that because you, you get the band more support. Always has just about a six piece, probably seven pieces on that truck. You play that, that style in order to give, give the band more support. That's, that's the only reason.
You caught it. Tailgate.
Oh. That's something you didn't shot at that. Yeah. Firecrackets. You'll find them someplace.
Yeah.
Um.
Now let's see about, let me go back to Buddy Petit, you know, but, um, just a moment. I'd like to keep... I'd like to keep... Yeah.

I only way, not personally myself, I only way have been trouble with Buddy. Nothing, you know, to, to complain about. Most anybody, during that time, would spend two, three dollars out of the deposit more than he should, see. But if a fella come up and tell you, say, well, I owe you a dollar, maybe a dollar and a half until the next job, because his occasion called for the use it, I would call that, you know, take nothing from a person. Oh. Well, that's the only, only time that I remember anything about Buddy or any, any one of them. Oh. They'd come up and tell me. But some of the boys say they'd play with him and jobs supposed to be paying so much money, and he'd tell him, uh, pay one, one, one price and the job would be paying another. See, well that's, if that happened, it didn't happen to me. Because if I go to work for a person, you come to hire me and say, well, you're waking tonight or tomorrow night? No. Say, well, I got a job, I can pay you four dollars. I'm looking for the four dollars. Oh. Now you can make forty-four. If you tell me you're going to pay me four dollars, that's all I'm looking. If you can make more than that, I wouldn't call that. Of course it, it, it, it doesn't fit in that way, see. In a way it is, take it. But, things like that would occur. People would tell me, see, but, but personally myself, it didn't happen to me that way. If it did, well then I always got my money, it happened once or twice, well I wouldn't do it.
I've heard people say that he was sort of unalable in some ways, you know, like people think he wouldn't show up.
Well, he'd do that in his own band. He would. He'd do that. See, when I, when the time he played with me, he was always right there. Well, he'd be half drunk or not, he'd be there.
Did he drink much? Yeah. Could he play alright when he was drinking? Yeah.

Until he got too sourced, well nobody would do nothing to get too much of it. He did pretty well. I loved pretty well. And most of the time he'd be paying for people and the people he's working for make him jump. So that, if I'm working for you, you paid me off and you keep insisting on me drinking, you know, like that, well then, you just as much support as I am for drinking, you know, that's speaking to you. Yeah. Especially if you know I'm drinking, we'll get overbalanced. Yeah. That's the way I figure about it. Yeah. Was he popular? Very popular. Around here? Yeah. Most popular's been around here for a couple of years after the kid ordered, I think. Yes. Yeah. He and Sam Morgan. Just about, just about 60, 60, 60. Oh. Being popular, most white and colored. Really? That's right. Did he play white songs? Yeah, sure. All of the better played white clubs. They were the best, best of them. We didn't do too much of this hotel work here like we do right now.
But the country clubs, yacht clubs, well a few hotels, but not, you know, as much as
much as you do. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. better class but you know the rich.
What was it about Buddy's band that made it popular?
Well they just naturally had a good band. They was together. They had wonderful trombone player. Zebra Norris was good. Good rhythm. Buddy was a good trumpet.

It wasn't too loud. Remember now who the other trumpet player was? You said you could something, maybe something in the order of Louie and somebody else and you couldn't remember who the other one was. Freddie Kaplan.
Oh Freddie Kaplan.
Did you hear him playing?

You were just on records. I was around Chicago. I wanted to get a chance to hear him but I never did. He was working in the loop at that time. I was only there for a couple of days. I didn't get a chance to hear him.
But did he have much of a reputation?

Yeah. Yeah, he had 20% reputation. He had to build for an arrangement to build for an There are age people that can't do that now. Younger class, there are a few of them, you know, go for it. But the people that go for it, most of the people, you know, middle-aged people, yes. Those are the people that support it now.

How do you like playing at Preservation Talk? All right. Good. I like it. I notice now when they play there, you know, there are always a lot of solos. Yeah. Is that something new that you used to play?

No, we didn't play. Well, yeah, that's the difference. They didn't play those. No. No. If you did, everybody played right along. The only time a musician would take down in the old days. Dry your lips or give your lip a rest or something like that. But all those solos, you know, each man took a solo. What I really need is from the Jitney dance. People do that in the Jitney dance because you're constantly playing in it. You're in there at 8.30. When you're kicked off, you don't stop the music until 1.30, 1 o'clock, can you? You couldn't play that thing as regular because you'd have to take that tape sometimes. What? You couldn't play that tape machine as long as we played in a Jitney dance because you'd have to take that tape. Yes, right. And the Jitney dance, you'd kick out and write all again. No force at all? No. Eat on the fly. Sure. Three hours in there, you're three hours of music going in there. When I was waking up. Of course, it might have changed after I left, but when I was
waking up, that's really right. Yeah. And so you wouldn't have solos in that? Yeah. Well,

you see, you'd have to take down, you know, one man's take down, and somebody's got to be down in order to pick up their next tune. So I imagine that's where all that would have reasoned. How do you like this business of having satellites down like they do? I think they have too many of them. I think it's monotonous in a way. Yes. It's a help to the musicians, but just, it's the same. Do you think that's why they do it? Yeah, that's why they do it, and then they want to give the individual, the musician a chance to show himself, see. That's one reason. But personally, myself, I don't like it. No. Because I'm not too much of a solo man. No. And I don't like it. No. That's
my, my business. I absolutely agree with you. You know, I agree with you. I think it gets monotonous

to hear it like that. Some of the fellas, they, they want to be shown. And naturally, the fellas try to play, a man taking a solo, and he tell you to get out of there. Well, that's the best work I have to do. I'll quickly get out. They'll tell me who wants to get out. I'll get out. Especially nowadays. But before I didn't mind. But the band's played, you know, like that. If you're going to, well, you're going to stick out, other bands get on there. But everybody's playing, you know. On there, you see. Might have one or two solo men in a band. But not everybody in a band. No. Did they ever have things like banjo solos and so on? Yeah, they had the, uh, banjo solos, but the rest of the band would play right along with them. But they'd get on there and play softened. Yeah. No takedown, you know. It's like drum and piano playing in, uh, who's ever taken a solo? It wasn't that way. I know you've noticed those old records like Joe Arnold's records. They play and all those photos. The band would be playing it. And on there. Gives a better foundation. And then it helps the fellow that's doing this solo. He could probably use more of his own stuff. But he's got somebody in the back. And see, if you happen to make one note all, the rest of the band's in there. Well, you can easily come back in on the right, right side. See, that's, that's my opinion about things. Tell me about what, uh, how we, um, did
you ever hear Jim Robinson playing from when you were young? Yeah. Sure. I used to play with, uh,

Isaiah Morgan's band. Young Sam Morgan. Yeah. And Jim used to give me lots of work. He used to work on the riverfront, I think. Yeah. And his band would go out of town, especially in the wintertime when I'd just come in there off the show or something like that. Well, he'd work with his band. Isaiah Morgan. Not Sam. Isaiah. Yeah. And the fellow just died
about two years. Yeah. How did he, did he play about the same memories he was
now? Yeah. Yeah. He played about the same. As far as I remember. Yeah. Because he was
on those records. Oh, sir. Seems like he's improved probably a lot, so

you see. That's my impression. Yeah, well, maybe so. You see, well, I don't, I, you see, you hear people play, and not often. You can't, you can't get much about it, but my opinion, you know, he's bound to improve because he's doing more playing out in there, you know, with different bands. Yeah. He played with different bands. Well, when he started, I don't know if I was the old, I wasn't a first band that I, that first band I remember him, being with them. Oh. I was in, and, same time as Morgan. How much are you paying now? You yourself? Oh, I don't do much paying. I play mostly with the best bands. Yeah. Now and then, I go down there and play with the loudest and the, mostly when Jim's out of town. Mm-hmm. I play with Preci, Preci, Preci, and sometimes. But other than that, I'm, you like to play? Yeah. But, I do most brass bands, like, like, like, you know, Preci's band, Eureka band, and then,
Morgan, you know, a good lot of work, and his, his band. Do you like this, the crossbones,

though? Yeah. Yeah, I like it. And then, not too long. Yeah. The long ones I can't make them anymore. Six to seven hours like that, I can't make those anymore. Oh, that's cool. No, it's presentation, you know, more, well, that's most what, most would get any
money out of it. How did you like your trip there? You just came back from Mexico. Tell, tell us about your trip to Mexico. Oh, it was lovely. What, what, what, what did you do,

about the most riding band? Yeah. In Mexico, we played a different corks. It's, uh, oh, it's a big park band. They claim it's seven wide, seven miles long. Beautiful place. We played a different section about three times at the, you know, different sections of that park, outdoors. And we played in an auditorium. Big auditorium. We did about, I'd say about two, two hours a day. On some occasion, one, one occasion, I think we doubled up, you know, and we did two in the, in the morning and two in the afternoon. Work wasn't all, and everybody was present. Good car, I said, oh, yeah. Good driving. We went about a hundred and fifty miles over to some other historical place in Mexico, out from Mexico City, way up in the clouds. Went there on a bus. That's the first time I've ever been in a bus above the clouds. Look down, and an airplane, you know, it's different. That's the first time I've been in a bus. Did you get to see any of the Olympics? No. See, where we were, we was just in the entertaining department, you know, just like singing and dancing, you know, from all over the world, all types of things. It's a thing. . . . . . .

segments.title: Buddy Petit joins Humphrey's band from Mandeville
segments.summary: Humphrey recalls Petit leaving Mandeville to join his band with Lee Collins for about two months around 1926, and names the personnel.

segments.title: Disagreement over how long he played with Petit
segments.summary: Allen's earlier account differs; Humphrey says he only substituted for Petit's sick trombonist before then.

segments.title: Personnel of Buddy Petit's own band
segments.summary: Humphrey lists the members of Petit's six-piece band, the most popular jazz band of the time.

segments.title: Freddie Keppard's trumpet style
segments.summary: Humphrey says the trumpeter was good, between Armstrong and Bunk Johnson in some phrases, with ideas of his own.

segments.title: Rumoured Petit recordings and country touring
segments.summary: Allen asks about possible home recordings; Humphrey says Petit travelled between towns and states on weekends.

segments.title: House band at the baseball park pavilion
segments.summary: Humphrey describes the Sunday job at a baseball park pavilion near the 17th Street Canal, where he managed Humpy's band.

segments.title: George Lewis in those days and dating the period
segments.summary: Humphrey says George Lewis was good then and has since improved his tone; they try to date it to 1924-27.

segments.title: Leaving in 1931 and when Buddy Petit died
segments.summary: Humphrey left March 31, 1931, Petit was still alive then, and he only heard of the death after returning in 1941.

segments.title: Slow blues that started fights at dances
segments.summary: Humphrey explains how a low-down blues played late in prohibition-era dances would provoke fights, and they hum it.

segments.title: Chris Kelly's playing and where they worked
segments.summary: Allen links the blues to Chris Kelly; Humphrey praises his style, tone and mutes and lists halls they played.

segments.title: Johnny Brown's band, Harrison and outstanding clarinetists
segments.summary: Humphrey says he subbed in Johnny Brown's band for trombonist Harrison of Algiers; Allen asks about top clarinetists.

segments.title: Why he left New Orleans and the Depression
segments.summary: Humphrey gives his reasons for leaving, better pay on the road, and says the Depression kept him away.

segments.title: Florida Blossom Minstrel Show
segments.summary: Humphrey describes three years with a tent minstrel show and its twelve-piece band, moving daily.

segments.title: Playing in Virginia and giving up trombone
segments.summary: Humphrey recalls switching from trombone and playing with combos and a bigger band around Charlottesville.

segments.title: Returning to New Orleans after his wife's death
segments.summary: He lost his wife in 1958, had a heart attack, and came home to help his family and join his brother's band.

segments.title: Changes in New Orleans and integration
segments.summary: Humphrey says the city has grown and integration has changed attitudes and living conditions.

segments.title: Music changes: Dixieland, modern jazz and rock
segments.summary: Humphrey says modern jazz and rock draw younger audiences while the old style is unchanged.

segments.title: Tape break
segments.summary: The tape runs out and they pause before the other side.

segments.title: Recording technology and how old records sound
segments.summary: Allen asks whether style changed; Humphrey says early recording lost bass and drums, which pushed use of sousaphone.

segments.title: Humphrey's own recording session
segments.summary: He recalls making a record but not the titles, and being asked to play again after construction work.

segments.title: Unrecorded bands and similarity of styles
segments.summary: Allen suggests unrecorded bands swung more; Humphrey says styles are similar but no two players alike.

segments.title: First jobs and the family band
segments.summary: Humphrey recalls his first job with guitarist Dan's lake-camp band and concerts with his grandfather.

segments.title: Manuel Perez and King Oliver
segments.summary: He worked with Perez for months and admired his tone; he was too young to hear King Oliver.

segments.title: Birth year and playing Pete Lala's cabaret
segments.summary: Born 1902, he played at Pete Lala's cabaret with Charlie Love and others.

segments.title: The trombone player he admired most
segments.summary: Humphrey praises a favourite trombonist's smooth style and faking, playing without reading.

segments.title: Singing trombone, tailgate and vamping
segments.summary: He explains the origin of tailgate from advertising trucks and the vamping bass style.

segments.title: Petit's reliability, pay and drinking
segments.summary: Humphrey says he had no trouble with Petit and was popular in white and Black clubs.

segments.title: What made Petit's band popular; Freddie Keppard
segments.summary: He says Petit's band was together with good rhythm and he only just missed hearing Keppard in Chicago.

segments.title: Solos and Jitney dance playing
segments.summary: Humphrey contrasts old ensemble playing for long dances with today's solos, which he finds monotonous.

segments.title: Jim Robinson, Isaiah Morgan and current playing
segments.summary: He recalls working in Isaiah Morgan's band, compares Robinson's playing, and says what bands he plays with now.

segments.title: Trip to Mexico
segments.summary: Humphrey describes performing at the Olympics cultural program in Mexico City.
